abstract: This paper investigates the widely held assumption that COVID-19 vaccine hesitancy in the US was driven primarily by social media misinformation. Using a combination of large-scale lab experiments, crowdsourcing, and machine learning, the authors estimate the causal impact of thousands of vaccine-related Facebook URLs on the vaccination intentions of roughly 233 million US users. They find that unflagged, non-'false' content that encouraged vaccine skepticism had a far larger aggregate effect on reducing vaccine uptake than outright misinformation flagged as false.
key_claims: The popular narrative attributing low COVID-19 vaccine uptake mainly to social media misinformation is incomplete or misleading.
Unflagged content that fostered vaccine skepticism, though not classified as false, had a substantially greater aggregate impact on vaccination intentions than explicitly flagged misinformation.
The impact of vaccine-skeptical unflagged content was estimated to be about 46 times greater than that of flagged misinformation.
methods: A framework combining lab experiments with a total N = 18,725 participants.
Machine learning to scale estimates across large numbers of URLs.
Causal estimation of the effect of 13,206 vaccine-related URLs on vaccination intentions.
Application to a population of approximately 233 million US Facebook users.
findings: Unflagged vaccine-skeptical content had roughly 46-fold greater impact on vaccination intentions than flagged misinformation.
The large aggregate effect of unflagged content stems from its far wider reach and exposure compared to flagged false content, despite lower per-exposure persuasive impact.
contributions: Introduces a scalable framework integrating experiments, crowdsourcing, and machine learning to estimate causal effects of online content at population scale.
Provides an empirical reframing of the misinformation-and-vaccination debate, emphasizing legal-but-skeptical content over overtly false content.
Quantifies the relative real-world impact of different categories of vaccine-related social media content.
framing: The paper situates itself within debates on misinformation, social media influence, and public health, challenging the dominant framing that focuses on flagged 'false' content. It advances a more nuanced view in which the reach of misleading-but-not-false content matters more than per-item falsity.
